opus-5.5.text:
I think the way I frame it is that a standard Transformer spends roughly the same amount of compute on every token, and that's clearly not how the problem is structured. Some tokens are trivial. Predicting the closing parenthesis, or the next word in a very common phrase, shouldn't cost the same as working through the hard step in a math proof. So a lot of what I find interesting is how you let the model decide where to spend its compute.

There are a few directions there. One is conditional computation, like mixture-of-experts, where you grow the number of parameters without growing the FLOPs per token proportionally. That's been very productive because it decouples capacity from cost. Another is adaptive depth, or early exiting, where easy tokens leave the network sooner. And the one everyone's thinking about now is test-time compute: letting the model think longer, generate intermediate reasoning, and essentially buy more serial computation when the problem calls for it.

The other side, which I care about a lot coming from optimization, is that architecture and optimizer aren't separate questions. You can have a beautiful architecture that's hard to train efficiently at scale. So when I think about using compute better, I'm also asking whether we're getting the most out of every training step. Better preconditioning, second-order-style methods like Shampoo, better handling of numerics and stability. If you can reach the same loss in fewer steps, that's a compute win just as real as an architectural trick.

And finally there's the hardware co-design angle. The things that win are often the ones that map well onto the accelerators we have: dense matmuls, good memory locality, communication patterns that scale. An idea that's theoretically efficient but fights the hardware usually loses in practice. So I try to keep all three of those in mind at once: what the model spends compute on, how efficiently we train it, and how well it runs on real systems.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it is that a Transformer spends the same amount of compute on every token, and that's almost certainly wrong. Some tokens are trivial, like finishing a common word or closing a parenthesis, and some are genuinely hard, where the model needs to actually reason. So the first lever is adaptivity: letting the network decide how much work to do per token, whether that's through mixture-of-experts routing, early exit, or mixture-of-depths style approaches where tokens can skip layers. You're trying to decouple the parameter count, which is about knowledge capacity, from the FLOPs you spend per token, which is about the difficulty of the prediction.

The second lever is more about where the compute actually goes on the hardware. People talk about FLOPs, but a lot of the time the accelerator is sitting idle waiting on memory bandwidth, especially with attention over long contexts and with the KV cache at inference time. So things like grouped-query attention, sparse or local attention patterns, and better fused kernels aren't glamorous architecture changes, but they can matter as much as anything on the modeling side, because they change the effective compute you get per dollar.

And the third piece, which I think gets underappreciated, is the optimizer and the training recipe. If you can get to the same loss in fewer steps with a better optimizer, or by shaping the data curriculum, that's compute efficiency too, just on the training side rather than the forward pass. My bias is that you have to evaluate all of these on a compute-matched basis. It's very easy to propose a clever architecture that looks great at a fixed parameter count but loses once you account for wall-clock time on real hardware. The honest comparison is always: for this many chip-hours, what's the best model you can get?

astra-6.text:
I think the interesting question is, how much computation do you actually need for a particular input? In a standard Transformer, you’re applying roughly the same amount of computation to every token. But some predictions are very easy, and others require substantially more work.

So one direction is conditional computation: activating only a subset of the model’s capacity for a given token. Mixture of experts is an example of that. You can increase the number of parameters without increasing the computation proportionally. But then you have to make that efficient on the hardware. Routing, communication, and load balancing can eat into the gains you see on paper.

Another direction is varying how much computation you spend on a problem. Can the model do a little work when the answer is straightforward and more work when it needs to reason? To me, that’s a compelling way to think about improving the architecture: not just making every operation cheaper, but learning where computation is useful.

sol-6.1.text:
I think about it in terms of how much useful work you get out of a fixed compute budget. A Transformer applies roughly the same amount of computation to every token, but some tokens—and some problems—need much more computation than others. So one direction is to make that allocation more adaptive: which parts of the model you activate, how much computation you spend, and where you spend it.

Then there’s the practical side. An architecture can look more efficient on paper and still run slower because it moves more data around or doesn’t map well to the hardware. So you have to look at the whole system and ask: for the same actual cost, are we getting a better model?
